title: Understanding the Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
We usually think that if everyone makes the best choice for themselves, the final result should also be good. However, this is not always true. The Prisoner’s Dilemma shows how two people can make rational choices but still end up with a worse result for both.
Imagine that two suspects, A and B, are arrested and questioned separately. They cannot talk to each other. Each person has two choices: stay silent or confess.
If both stay silent, they each spend one year in prison. If one confesses and the other stays silent, the person who confesses goes free, while the other person spends five years in prison. If both confess, they each spend three years in prison.
\[\begin{array}{c|cc}
& \text{B Stays Silent} & \text{B Confesses} \\
\hline
\text{A Stays Silent} & (1,1) & (5,0) \\
\text{A Confesses} & (0,5) & (3,3)
\end{array}\] Now think about the situation from A’s point of view. If B stays silent, A should confess because going free is better than spending one year in prison. If B confesses, A should still confess because three years in prison is better than five years.
So, no matter what B does, confessing is the better choice for A. B will think in the same way. In the end, both of them confess and each spends three years in prison.
But this creates a strange result. If both of them had stayed silent, they would have spent only one year in prison. They both made the best choice for themselves, but they ended up with a worse result.
This is what makes the Prisoner’s Dilemma interesting. Neither person is making a bad decision. From each person’s point of view, confessing makes sense. The problem is that when both people make the same rational choice, the final result is worse for both of them.
We can also see this idea in economics. Imagine two companies selling similar products. Both companies can keep their prices high or lower their prices. If both keep their prices high, they can both make good profits. However, each company has a reason to lower its price. If the other company keeps a high price, lowering the price may attract more customers. If the other company lowers its price, the company may also need to lower its price to avoid losing customers.
As a result, both companies may lower their prices and start a price war. In the end, both companies may make less profit. Just like the two prisoners, each company is trying to make the best decision for itself, but the final result can be worse for everyone.
The main lesson of the Prisoner’s Dilemma is simple: the best choice for each person is not always the best choice for the group. It also helps explain why cooperation can be difficult. Even when cooperation could make everyone better off, people may still have a reason to choose what is best for themselves.

title: What Can $20 Buy? Choosing a Dining Days Meal
text:
The group chat has agreed on dinner. Now someone wants Indian food, someone else wants Thai, and nobody wants to spend too much. A long restaurant list helps, but it does not answer the next question: would a bigger budget give us more places we actually want to try?
I looked at the 2026 University City Dining Days event, where restaurants offered set menus at $20, $30, and $40. My question is whether spending more, or meeting for lunch, adds choices for a particular cuisine. For a student, another $10 per person is not a small change. For four friends, it adds $40 before tax and tips. The useful comparison is therefore what that extra money makes possible, not just which price group has the longest list. I compare two decisions: keeping the meal time and raising the budget, or keeping the budget and meeting earlier. Neither helps unless it adds something the group wants.
I used R and rvest to collect names, meal types, prices, and links from the official participant list, first accessed on September 19, 2026. The saved list has 44 restaurant–meal–price entries. I removed extra spaces and checked duplicates within each group. Cafe deals are left out. For this closer look, I selected seven restaurants with Indian, Thai, or Chinese menus and checked their linked menus on October 7. These are examples to help make a shortlist, not a complete guide to every cuisine in the event.
Each bar counts restaurants whose cheapest listed menu fits the budget. A $40 budget includes $20 and $30 menus too. The cuisine labels are broad groups I added from the menus, rather than labels collected from the main page. The code joins these notes to the scraped list and counts each restaurant once per meal and budget. This separates access to another restaurant from paying for another menu at the same place.
For Indian food, lunch makes a difference at $20. Both New Delhi and Desi Chaat House fit that lunch budget, while only New Delhi fits it at dinner. Desi Chaat House joins the dinner shortlist at $30. Within these examples, raising the dinner budget from $20 to $30 adds 1 restaurant; raising it again to $40 adds none. Switching to lunch at $20 reaches the same two restaurants without that higher menu budget. But lunch is not simply the same meal for less: its lunch choices focus on chaat, while dinner includes curry and biryani. I would choose lunch if I wanted chaat and a smaller bill, rather than expect an identical dinner deal.
For Thai food, the two places reviewed, Pattaya and Thai Singha House, already have $20 options at both meals. Raising the budget adds no restaurant in this pair. It can still change what you eat. Thai Singha House also lists a $30 menu with seafood or duck choices, although the main page only puts it in the $20 group. Here the choice is about dishes, not access to another place. I would keep a $20 budget unless someone specifically wanted the more expensive menu.
For Chinese food, Sangkee offers a $20 starting point at either meal. At $40, Dim Sum House adds another place for lunch or dinner, and Han Dynasty adds a dinner choice. This gives the reviewed Chinese dinner shortlist 3 restaurants. Dim Sum House’s lunch appears on its menu but is missing from the main lunch list. I recorded this difference instead of assuming that the main page was complete. In this shortlist, the first extra $10 adds no Chinese restaurant at dinner, but the next $10 adds 2. That is a reason to consider $40 if someone wants those particular places, not evidence that $40 meals taste better.
These are historical event menus, not current deals. I kept the saved data so running the analysis does not repeatedly download pages; the optional scraper requests one public page without bypassing restrictions. The seven examples were selected for this comparison, not sampled randomly. Their counts cannot rank all cuisines or represent the whole neighborhood. Prices exclude tax, tips, and some optional extras. Nothing here measures food quality or guarantees a table.

title: Which Dining Days Option Offers the Most Restaurant Choices?
text:
When choosing a restaurant, people often think about the price and whether they want lunch or dinner. In this post, I ask: Which meal and price group had the most restaurant choices during University City Dining Days in 2026? I use R and rvest to compare lunch and dinner at $20, $30, and $40.
The data come from the official Dining Days page, which I accessed on September 19, 2026. The page lists restaurants from the 2026 event and says the next event will be in July 2027. This post looks at the 2026 list. It does not mean these deals are available now.

Takeaway and limitations
For this 2026 list, diners seeking the widest selection at an exact price tier would start with $40 dinner. With a $20 menu budget and flexible timing, lunch offers more choices. At lunch, paying $40 instead of $30 sharply narrows the list; a higher price is not evidence of better value.

The class selectors and results must be rechecked if the website changes. For a future visit, use this comparison to plan a shortlist, then confirm the next event’s participants, menus, and hours before booking.

Based on the 2026 list, I would suggest $40 dinner to someone who wants the most choices within one meal and price group. For someone with a $20 menu budget who can choose either meal, lunch has more options. For lunch, the $30 group has more choices than the $40 group. title: Education and Unemployment in the United States
text:
A degree takes years of work, and often a lot of money. One reason to keep going is the hope of having more job options afterward. But how closely is education related to unemployment? And does looking only at people in the labor force leave out part of the story?
I start with unemployment over time, then compare people of similar ages. Finally, I look beyond unemployment to include people outside the labor force. Each view answers a different question: is the gap persistent, does it remain within age groups, and who is missing from the unemployment rate?
The data come from IPUMS CPS, using Basic Monthly January samples for 2020–2026. I focus on civilians ages 25–64, since many younger people are still in school and some older people have retired. “Some college” includes associate degrees; “bachelor’s or higher” includes graduate degrees.
I use the person weight WTFINL because each survey respondent represents a different number of people. The unemployment rate is the weighted share of the labor force who are unemployed, including people looking for work or on temporary layoff. The final chart has a different denominator: all civilians ages 25–64 in each education group.
The gap is not just a feature of one month. The bachelor’s-or-higher group has the lowest unemployment rate in every January shown. All four groups had higher rates in January 2021 than in January 2020, followed by declines in 2022 and 2023. In January 2026, the rate was 7.4% for people without a high school diploma and 3% for those with a bachelor’s degree or higher.
Education seems related to how exposed people are to unemployment, even as the labor market changes. But these are January snapshots, not annual averages or seasonally adjusted rates. January 2020 was before the major pandemic changes, so the graph misses what happened later that year.
Could the gap simply reflect age? Education groups may contain different shares of younger and older workers, who also have different experience. The next chart compares education groups within the same ten-year age band.
The main pattern remains within all four age groups: people with a bachelor’s degree or higher have lower unemployment than those with only high school or less. Among ages 25–34, the gap between the lowest and highest education groups is about 8.3 percentage points. It is smaller, but still present, in the older groups.
This matters for the original question. The overall education gap is not explained only by different age mixes across education groups. The ranking is not perfectly step-by-step: among ages 55–64, some college and bachelor’s-or-higher rates are very close. Comparing age bands also does not hold jobs, experience, or family circumstances constant.
There is another limit to unemployment rates: people outside the labor force are not counted. The final chart brings them back in.
About 58.2% of adults without a high school diploma were employed, compared with 84.8% of those with a bachelor’s degree or higher. The shares outside the labor force were 37.2% and 12.6%, respectively. The orange segments are shares of all adults, so they are not the unemployment rates in the first two charts.
The difference in employment is therefore broader than unemployment alone suggests. People outside the labor force may be studying, caring for family, retired, or unable to work. They should not all be treated as unsuccessful job seekers.

title: Education and Unemployment in the United States
text:
Does more education go with lower unemployment? I wanted to look at this question because education is often related to the types of jobs people can get. At the same time, education is not the only thing that matters. People with different education levels may also have different jobs and work experience.
In this post, I use IPUMS CPS data to compare unemployment across four education groups. I first look at January 2026, then compare January samples from 2020 to 2026. Finally, I look at different age groups to see if the same pattern still appears.

title: Education and Unemployment in the United States
text:
Data and method
The data come from the IPUMS Current Population Survey. I use the Basic Monthly January sample from each year between 2020 and 2026. I focus on civilians ages 25–64 who are in the labor force. I chose this age range because many younger people are still in school, while some older people have already retired.

I use EMPSTAT to identify employed and unemployed people, and EDUC to group education. People who are not in the labor force are excluded. Some college includes an associate degree. The highest group includes bachelor’s and graduate degrees.

workers <- cps |>
  filter(
    YEAR >= 2020, YEAR <= 2026, MONTH == 1,
    AGE >= 25, AGE <= 64, WTFINL > 0,
    EMPSTAT %in% c(10, 12, 20, 21, 22)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      EDUC %in% c(2, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 71) ~ "Less than high school",
      EDUC == 73 ~ "High school",
      EDUC %in% c(81, 91, 92) ~ "Some college / associate",
      EDUC %in% c(111, 123, 124, 125) ~ "Bachelor's or higher"
    ),
    unemployed = EMPSTAT %in% c(20, 21, 22),
    age_group = case_when(
      AGE < 35 ~ "25-34",
      AGE < 45 ~ "35-44",
      AGE < 55 ~ "45-54",
      TRUE ~ "55-64"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(education)) |>
  mutate(
    education = factor(education, levels = c(
      "Less than high school", "High school",
      "Some college / associate", "Bachelor's or higher"
    ))
  )

Since the CPS is a survey, each person in the sample can represent a different number of people in the U.S. population. I use the Basic Monthly person weight, WTFINL, when calculating unemployment rates. The unemployment rate here is the share of people in the labor force who are unemployed, expressed as a percentage.

rates <- workers |>
  group_by(YEAR, education) |>
  summarise(
    sample_n = n(),
    rate = 100 * weighted.mean(unemployed, WTFINL),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

title: Education and Employment in the United States
text:
Takeaway and limits
Higher education was generally associated with lower unemployment across years and age groups. However, these comparisons do not separate education from differences in occupation, experience, or other factors. Small differences should also be read carefully because the CPS is a sample, especially within smaller age and education groups. These charts show estimates, not tests of statistical significance.
The main takeaway is that the education gap is persistent, but its size varies by age and year. Education is one useful part of understanding unemployment, rather than a guarantee of employment.

title: Two Kinds of Gas: Different Prices, Different Risks
text:
A higher price at the gas station is easy to notice. But does it mean natural gas is becoming more expensive too? Both fuels are often called “gas,” which makes it tempting to talk about them as one energy cost. They are different products, and treating one as a guide to the other could give the wrong picture.
I wanted to separate two questions: which fuel became more expensive after inflation, and which had larger changes from month to month? The difference matters for planning costs. A price can be low compared with the past but still change sharply next month. A business that uses natural gas needs to understand its own price pattern, rather than assume that lower gasoline prices mean lower energy costs everywhere.
I use U.S. regular gasoline and Henry Hub natural gas prices from January 2000 to August 2026. The data come from the Energy Information Administration through FRED: gasoline and natural gas. R code downloaded monthly averages through the API. I matched the months and used the Consumer Price Index to adjust for inflation. I first look at each fuel’s price history. Then I compare their inflation-adjusted changes using a common index. Finally, I compare monthly price swings to see whether a lower long-term price also means more stability.
Gasoline’s highest monthly dollar price was $4.93 per gallon in June 2022. It ended at $4.06 in August 2026. For a driver buying the same number of gallons, a higher price means a larger payment. It does not tell us whether that payment takes a larger share of income, since income and fuel use are not in these data.
Natural gas reached its highest monthly dollar price earlier: $13.43 in October 2005. It also rose around 2008 and 2022, but neither increase reached that earlier record. Its August 2026 price was $2.79 per million BTU. So the largest increases did not happen at the same time for both fuels.
The different peak years show that the two markets did not have the same price history. But gasoline is measured in dollars per gallon and natural gas in dollars per million BTU, so their dollar prices cannot be compared directly. Gasoline is also a retail pump price including taxes, while Henry Hub is a wholesale benchmark, not a household heating bill. To compare how prices changed, I adjust for inflation and set both indexes to 100 in January 2000.
I put both prices in August 2026 dollars, then set each fuel’s January 2000 real price to 100. An index of 150 means a price 50% above its own starting point after inflation. By August 2026, gasoline was about 59% above its starting level, while natural gas was about 41% below. These are changes from a chosen month, not a comparison of energy costs per unit of heat.
Inflation also changes the gasoline story. Its real-price peak came in 2008, even though its dollar-price peak came in 2022. A record pump price is not necessarily a record relative to other goods and services.
A lower long-term price did not make natural gas more stable. Across 315 matched monthly changes, its average change in either direction was 11.6%, compared with 4.5% for gasoline. I take absolute values before averaging, so rises and falls do not cancel. The boxes show the middle half of changes, with the line inside marking the median. The wider spread for natural gas shows why its lower ending price alone says little about short-term uncertainty.
The fuels moved in the same direction in only about 52% of those months. Their monthly-change correlation was 0.03, close to zero. Shared peaks in a few years therefore do not mean that their month-to-month changes generally matched.
These results describe this sample, not a forecast or a causal relationship. The series are not seasonally adjusted, and monthly averages hide shorter spikes. Missing natural gas in March 2004 and CPI in October 2025 remain blank. For changes, I exclude a month if either fuel lacks the current or previous real price, using the same months for both fuels.

title: Two Kinds of Gas: Different Prices, Different Risks
text:
Takeaway
From January 2000 to August 2026, gasoline became more expensive after inflation, while natural gas ended lower but had larger monthly price swings. A lower price over the long run did not mean a more stable price from month to month.
For a business planning energy costs, this means checking both the long-term change and short-term swings in the fuel it actually uses. Lower natural gas prices alone are not a reason to expect stable future costs, and gasoline prices are not a reliable guide to natural gas prices in this sample. Actual bills also depend on usage and other charges, so these price patterns are a starting point for planning, not a forecast.

title: What a Statewide Income Number Misses in Texas
text:
How much does a typical Texas household earn? A single number gives a quick answer, but Texas is a large state. It seems unlikely that the same number describes a household near Dallas and one near the southern border equally well. I wanted to see where higher and lower household incomes are located, and what we miss when we use the state as one unit. In particular, I look at whether income differences appear across regions and even between counties near the same major city.
This matters when deciding where to look more closely at local needs. A county below the state income level may deserve a different set of questions about jobs, housing, or services than a county far above it. A map cannot decide where funding should go, but it can show differences that a statewide number hides.
I use the Census Bureau’s 2020–2024 ACS five-year estimates, table B19013. The measure is median household income: the middle of the household income distribution, not an individual salary or the mean household income. Values are in 2024 dollars. These estimates combine five years of survey data, so they do not describe only households surveyed in 2024.
I used R to get income estimates from the Census API and read the 2024 county boundaries. I selected Texas and matched the two datasets by county ID. I used tmap for the saved map and Leaflet for the interactive version below. All 254 counties matched, with no missing income estimates. The map uses the same dollar scale across the state; darker counties have higher estimated medians.
Zoom in to explore an area and click a county to see its income estimate and margin of error. County size shows land area, not population.
Open the interactive map in a new page · View the static map
The darker areas are concentrated in several places rather than spread evenly across Texas. Collin and Denton, north of Dallas, both have median household incomes above $100,000. Another high-income area appears around Austin, including Travis and Williamson. Fort Bend, southwest of Houston, also stands out. These examples show where some higher-income counties are located. They do not compare all urban and rural counties or show that living near a city causes higher income.
Farther south, Starr, Hidalgo, and Cameron form a neighboring group with lower estimates. Starr’s median is $37,639, compared with the Texas median of $78,476. Hidalgo and Cameron are higher than Starr, but both remain below the state figure. This is more useful than identifying one low-income county: it points to a broader area where local conditions deserve attention. The data alone cannot tell us why these differences exist.
The large pale counties in western Texas need careful reading too. They occupy much of the map, but land area is not the number of people living there. Also, 213 of the 254 county estimates are below the state median. That does not mean the same fraction of Texas households has below-median income. Counties have different numbers of households, and the statewide median is not the average of county medians.
The second figure makes nearby differences easier to see. Collin’s median is $121,600, while Dallas County’s is $76,547. Fort Bend is also above Harris County, which contains much of Houston. A broad label such as “the Dallas area” or “the Houston area” would hide these contrasts.
This matters because counties in the same metropolitan area may have different income levels and local needs. Using only one regional number could hide these differences when studying housing affordability or access to services. However, income alone cannot tell us which county has greater needs. The ten counties are selected examples, not a random sample or a ranking of every county.
The bars extend one published margin of error on each side of the estimate, showing the Census Bureau’s 90% confidence intervals. Estimates are not exact, so small color differences should not become firm rankings. Glasscock is a useful warning: its estimated median exceeds $100,000, but its margin of error is about $53,000. A dark county is not always a precisely measured high-income county.
Income also does not measure living standards by itself. These estimates do not adjust for local housing costs or household size, and county medians hide differences within counties. Explaining the pattern would require more information about residents and local economies.

title: What a Statewide Income Number Misses in Texas
text:
Takeaway
A single statewide income number hides important differences across Texas. The map shows higher-income areas around several major cities and a lower-income group along part of the southern border. The county comparison also shows that incomes can differ widely even within the same metropolitan area.
These findings matter because local economic conditions cannot always be understood from state or regional averages. However, income alone does not tell us why these differences exist or which communities need more support. I would use this map as a starting point, then look at smaller areas, housing costs, and the uncertainty in the estimates before making decisions.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text: As I get ready to look for a job, I wonder what a first salary can tell me. One year may be unusual because of unemployment or a bonus. This matters for intergenerational mobility: how closely children’s economic outcomes are connected to their parents’. If one unusual year stands in for usual earnings, we may misread that connection. Does using three years instead of one change the estimated link between fathers’ and children’s earnings?

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Following Families Over Time
I use the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID): its 2023 Parent Identification File, 1968–2023 Individual File, and a family income extract. I study birth fathers because the first two income waves contain only Head earnings, limiting coverage of mothers. The measure is individual labor income, excluding farm and unincorporated business income—not total household income.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: How SQL Connects Fathers and Children
text:
How SQL Connects Fathers and Children
Python reads the needed columns using PSID’s supplied file layouts and loads them into SQLite. The Python code records the full variable mapping; the SQL file performs the matching and aggregation.
First, permanent individual IDs identify biological father–child links. The Individual File then locates each person’s family and role in each wave. SQL uses SELECT to choose fields and JOIN to connect records using both interview year and family interview number. A family number alone cannot identify someone across years. Without these joins, the income records would not tell us which father belongs to which child.
Income belongs to the person in the corresponding role: Reference Person earnings go only to the current Reference Person, and Spouse/Partner earnings only to that person. Other household members do not receive these earnings. Duplicate-key checks guard against counting a person twice.
Next, WHERE selects valid ages and positive earnings. GROUP BY gathers each person’s years, and AVG calculates their mean. Finally, another JOIN attaches father and child summaries to their biological link. I record counts for each matching and filtering step in the sample-count table, so readers can follow how the sample was built. The father and child counts describe separate groups, not consecutive steps in one shrinking sample.
For a fictional teaching example, not used in the analysis, suppose parent_links connects father 101 to child 205. Joining father 101 to father_means adds $50,000; joining child 205 to child_means adds $40,000. The resulting row contains both IDs and their separate average earnings.
The first query calculates three-year father averages from the correctly assigned, inflation-adjusted earnings records:
SELECT person, AVG(real_income) AS father_mean,
       COUNT(DISTINCT year) AS income_years
FROM earnings
WHERE year IN (2010, 2012, 2014)
  AND age BETWEEN 35 AND 60 AND real_income > 0
GROUP BY person
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT year) = 3;
HAVING requires three distinct years, so one available observation cannot pass as a multi-year average. After building both summaries, the second query links them:
SELECT l.child, l.father, f.father_mean, c.child_mean
FROM parent_links AS l
JOIN father_means AS f ON l.father = f.person
JOIN child_means AS c ON l.child = c.person
WHERE l.child <> l.father;
Here, l, f, and c are short table names. These inner joins exclude pairs missing either income summary. Checking the remaining sample size is therefore essential. Earlier in the saved SQL, the individual-to-family join uses p.wave = f.wave AND p.family = f.family before assigning earnings by role.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Does Averaging Earnings Change the Result?
text:
Does Averaging Earnings Change the Result?
I use father income in 2010/2012/2014 and child income in 2018/2020/2022. Fathers must be aged 35–60 and children 30–50 at every corresponding interview, which reports the previous year’s income. Requiring all six positive observations leaves 336 pairs and 238 fathers. I convert earnings to 2022 dollars using annual averages of BLS CPI from FRED, then average before taking logs.
I estimate intergenerational earnings elasticity (IGE):
\[
\log(Y_{\text{child}})=\alpha+\beta\log(Y_{\text{father}})+u
\]
Here, \(\beta\) measures the earnings association. A larger value means less relative mobility in this sample, not a causal effect or a measure of whether children earn more dollars.



Single-year and three-year-average IGE for the same 336 pairs. Dots show IGE estimates, and horizontal lines show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, resampling fathers and keeping siblings together.


Using father earnings in 2012 and child earnings in 2020 gives 0.234, versus 0.226 for three-year averages. Approximately, a 10% difference in fathers’ earnings is associated with a 2.3% difference in children’s earnings under either measure.
I expected averaging to change more. The difference is -0.008, with a 95% interval of -0.084 to 0.050. It is small and not statistically distinguishable from zero. Averaging can reduce temporary fluctuations, but need not increase the estimate in every sample.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Does the Choice of Year Matter?
text:
Does the Choice of Year Matter?



Nine single-year IGE estimates using the same complete pairs. Rows vary father income years; columns vary child income years.


Changing the income years moves the estimate from 0.150 to 0.240, even with identical people. Individual earnings changes and calendar-year conditions—including 2020—can affect the comparison. These point estimates show sensitivity; they do not establish that every difference is significant.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Why Age Matters
A young worker’s earnings may poorly represent their later position, especially when education or training delays earnings growth. Measuring children early can therefore understate their later earnings link with parents: a potential life-cycle bias. Averaging several early-career years may still miss long-run status.



Life-cycle comparison for 140 identical pairs, holding father earnings at the same three-year average.


I select 140 children from the main sample with positive 2014 earnings and ages 22–29 at the 2015 interview. These children meet the main sample’s age requirements at the 2019, 2021, and 2023 interviews, which report income for 2018, 2020, and 2022. They were younger at the 2015 interview reporting their 2014 earnings. Their mean interview age rises from 27.5 to 35.5 by 2023. IGE rises from 0.186 to 0.244, and median real earnings from $39,559 to $55,000.
This is descriptive evidence consistent with possible life-cycle bias, not statistical confirmation. The change’s 95% interval, -0.111 to 0.232, includes zero. Age and calendar time change together, so I cannot attribute the increase to aging alone. Averaging reduces temporary variation; it does not eliminate life-cycle bias.
These unweighted estimates describe selected positive earners with complete records, not all U.S. families. Attrition, PSID income imputations, changing family roles, and unequal parental and child ages also limit interpretation. They are not causal estimates.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Takeaway
I began by wondering what my first salary would say about my future. In this sample, the father-child earnings link looks stronger with a three-year average than with one year, although the evidence for a difference is uncertain. Measuring both generations at similar ages and averaging several years can each help with a different problem, but neither captures a whole career. I learned that before using IGE to describe mobility, we need to ask whose earnings we measure and when.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 1. Download the PSID Data
Register with PSID and obtain three inputs: Parent Identification 2023, Cross-Year Individual 1968–2023, and a family labor-income extract from the Data Center. Follow PSID’s data-use conditions; do not share the raw records.
Use the Blog 6 repository for the process files. Put the two unpacked folders and the income workbook in data/raw/. Its data instructions list exact filenames and variables. Keep PSID’s .do layouts with the TXT files.
The extract covers income years 2010–2022 at two-year intervals. I use fathers because 2010 and 2012 include only Head earnings; later waves also include Spouse/Partner earnings. The measure is individual labor income excluding farm and unincorporated business income, not household income.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Step 2. Prepare the Data in Python
text:
Step 2. Prepare the Data in Python
The Python script reads only needed fixed-width columns using the .do positions. Permanent IDs combine the original family ID and person number. These remain distinct from each wave’s family interview number.
The preparation code builds four data frames:







Python object
Contents




people
Person ID, interview year, family ID, sequence, role, age


links
Child ID and biological father ID


family
Interview year, family ID, Reference Person and Spouse earnings


annual
Annual CPI and conversion factor to 2022 dollars



After creating these frames, the script loads them into SQLite and executes the saved queries:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
for name, df in [("people", people), ("parent_links", links),
                 ("family_income", family), ("cpi", annual)]:
    df.to_sql(name, con, index=False)

con.executescript((POST / "sql/build_sample.sql").read_text())
sample = pd.read_sql_query(
    "SELECT * FROM matched_pairs ORDER BY child", con
)
Here, POST is the project folder determined by the script. This excerpt needs the prepared frames; it is not a standalone cell to run first. SQLite handles matching and averaging; Python retrieves the matched sample for regression and figures. Steps 3–4 explain the SQL file executed above.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Step 3. Match Parents and Children with SQL
text:
Step 3. Match Parents and Children with SQL
The parent file identifies who belongs to whom. The individual file locates each person’s family and role across waves. SELECT chooses the fields; JOIN connects the records. The first income join uses both interview year and family interview number:
FROM people AS p
JOIN family_income AS f
  ON p.wave = f.wave AND p.family = f.family
This is the matching clause from the earnings query. Family number alone is insufficient across years. The query assigns Reference Person earnings only to the current Reference Person, and Spouse/Partner earnings only to that role. Other household members do not inherit these earnings.
For a fictional teaching example, father 101 and child 205 appear together in parent_links. After Step 4 creates income summaries, the following join attaches their separate averages—say $50,000 and $40,000. These example values are not PSID observations or regression inputs.
SELECT l.child, l.father, f.father_mean, c.child_mean
FROM parent_links AS l
JOIN father_means AS f ON l.father = f.person
JOIN child_means AS c ON l.child = c.person
WHERE l.child <> l.father;
Without these joins, income records would not tell us which father belongs to which child. Inner joins exclude pairs missing either summary. I check duplicate identifiers and save sample counts; father and child eligibility counts describe separate groups, not a single shrinking funnel.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Step 4. Calculate Single-Year and Average Earnings
text:
Step 4. Calculate Single-Year and Average Earnings
I convert earnings to 2022 dollars using annual BLS CPI from FRED. WHERE filters observations, GROUP BY gathers each person’s years, and AVG calculates their mean:
SELECT person, AVG(real_income) AS father_mean,
       COUNT(DISTINCT year) AS income_years
FROM earnings
WHERE year IN (2010, 2012, 2014)
  AND age BETWEEN 35 AND 60 AND real_income > 0
GROUP BY person
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT year) = 3;
HAVING requires three distinct valid years. The child query uses 2018/2020/2022 and ages 30–50. Ages refer to interviews reporting the previous year’s income. All six earnings observations must be positive; missing and zero earnings do not enter the log regressions.
The full query also retains individual-year values using MAX(CASE WHEN year = ... THEN real_income END). Its final match gives 336 pairs and 238 fathers. Both main comparisons use these same people. The single-year measure uses father 2012 and child 2020 earnings; the multi-year measure averages each generation’s three real earnings observations before taking logs.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 5. Estimate Intergenerational Elasticity
The model is:
\[
\log(Y_{\text{child}})=\alpha+\beta\log(Y_{\text{father}})+u
\]
The IGE, \(\beta\), measures an association, not causation. A larger value means less relative mobility in this sample. The script calculates the ordinary least-squares slope with an intercept:
import numpy as np

def slope(x, y):
    x = np.log(np.asarray(x))
    y = np.log(np.asarray(y))
    return float(np.sum((x-x.mean()) * (y-y.mean()))
                 / np.sum((x-x.mean())**2))

single = slope(sample["f2012"], sample["c2020"])
averaged = slope(sample["father_mean"], sample["child_mean"])



Single-year and three-year-average IGE. Dots show estimates; horizontal lines show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, resampling fathers with their children.


The estimates are 0.234 and 0.226: a 10% father-earnings difference is associated with roughly a 2.3% child-earnings difference. Averaging changes the estimate by only -0.008, with a 95% interval of -0.084 to 0.050. This does not establish a difference between the measures.



Nine single-year estimates for the same complete pairs, varying father and child income years.


Across income-year choices, estimates range from 0.150 to 0.240. Earnings shocks and calendar-year conditions can change the picture, although these point estimates do not establish that every difference is significant.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 6. Check for Life-Cycle Bias
Young workers’ earnings may not reflect their later position, especially when training delays earnings growth. Measuring children early can therefore understate their later earnings link with parents. Averaging several early-career years does not necessarily solve this problem.
I select 140 of the main-sample children with positive 2014 earnings and interview ages 22–29 in 2015. They meet the main age restrictions at the later 2019/2021/2023 interviews. Father earnings remain the same three-year average.



The same 140 father–child pairs using child earnings at two career stages.


Mean interview age rises from 27.5 to 35.5, while IGE rises from 0.186 to 0.244. Median real earnings rise from $39,559 to $55,000. This demonstrates how changing measurement age and year can change the estimate for the same people.
The pattern is descriptive evidence consistent with potential life-cycle bias, not statistical confirmation. The change’s interval, -0.111 to 0.232, includes zero. Age and calendar time change together, so the increase cannot be attributed to aging alone.

section: Step 7. Interpret and Reproduce the Results
text:
Step 7. Interpret and Reproduce the Results
From the independent blog6 project folder, use a Python environment with the packages in requirements.txt. Run the complete script in Terminal:

The README includes environment setup and Jupyter instructions. Results and three figures are saved under results/; original inputs stay unchanged. The website copy generates the article too, while the independent repository reproduces only the analysis.

My takeaway is that multiple years can better represent usual earnings by reducing temporary fluctuations, but they do not reveal lifetime income or remove life-cycle bias. Averaging barely changes this sample’s main estimate. I would still avoid judging mobility from one convenient year: the matching, measurement ages, and people excluded matter too.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 1. Download the Data
I use the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), which follows people and families over time. After registering, download the 2023 Parent Identification File and the 1968–2023 Cross-Year Individual File. In the Data Center, select family labor-income variables for the 2011, 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023 survey waves. These interviews report earnings from the previous year. Save the files in your project folder and follow PSID’s data-use conditions. The data README lists the exact variables; the downloaded 2017 wave is not used in this analysis.
These files tell us who belongs to whom, where each person lived in each survey year, and how much they earned. I focus on birth fathers because my earliest income extracts include only Head earnings. The income measure excludes farm and unincorporated business income.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Step 2. Prepare the Data with Python
text:
Step 2. Prepare the Data with Python
I use Python to organize the data. For each person, I need a permanent ID, an interview year, a family ID, age, family role, and earnings. I also need a table linking children to their fathers. The supplied .do files give the column positions Python needs to read the TXT files.
After preparing the tables, I load them into SQLite. Here is a short example using the father–child links:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
links.to_sql("parent_links", con, index=False)
linked_ids = pd.read_sql_query(
    "SELECT child, father FROM parent_links", con
)
Here, links is the father–child table prepared from PSID. SELECT chooses the columns to return. The full analysis loads the other tables too: SQL does the matching and averaging, and Python calculates the IGE. The full Python and SQL code includes the preparation steps.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Step 3. Match Fathers and Children with SQL
text:
Step 3. Match Fathers and Children with SQL
Now I need to connect each child’s earnings to their father’s earnings. Permanent person IDs identify the biological relationship. To find each person’s income, I also match interview year and family interview number. A family number alone cannot track a person across years.
This short query shows the individual-to-family matching keys:
SELECT p.person, p.wave, p.family
FROM people AS p
JOIN family_income AS f
  ON p.wave = f.wave
 AND p.family = f.family;
I match both the interview year and family ID because the same family number may appear in different survey years. This query shows the connection only; assigning earnings also requires each person’s family role.
The family role matters: Reference Person earnings belong only to the current Reference Person, and Spouse/Partner earnings only to that person. I do not give everyone in a household the same earnings.
Once Step 4 creates the income summaries, this query connects them:
SELECT l.child, l.father, f.father_mean, c.child_mean
FROM parent_links AS l
JOIN father_means AS f ON l.father = f.person
JOIN child_means AS c ON l.child = c.person
WHERE l.child <> l.father;
For a fictional teaching example, suppose father 101 belongs to child 205. The first JOIN adds father 101’s average earnings of $50,000; the second adds child 205’s $40,000. These are made-up values, not observations used in the analysis. Without the joins, the income records would not tell us which father belongs to which child.
I check the matches and keep pairs with enough income information for both people. These inner joins leave out pairs missing either summary.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 4. Calculate Average Income
To compare years fairly, I first convert earnings to 2022 dollars using BLS CPI from FRED. Then I calculate each father’s average:
SELECT person, AVG(real_income) AS father_mean
FROM earnings
WHERE year IN (2010, 2012, 2014)
  AND age BETWEEN 35 AND 60 AND real_income > 0
GROUP BY person
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT year) = 3;
WHERE selects the years, ages, and positive earnings. GROUP BY collects each person’s observations, and AVG averages them. HAVING requires three distinct years, so one available year cannot count as a three-year average.
I use child earnings in 2018/2020/2022 and ages 30–50. Ages refer to the interviews reporting the previous year’s earnings. Requiring all six positive observations leaves 336 pairs and 238 fathers. Both comparisons use these same people.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 5. Compare the IGE Estimates
IGE measures how strongly children’s earnings are associated with their fathers’ earnings:
\[
\log(Y_{\text{child}})=\alpha+\beta\log(Y_{\text{father}})+u
\]
The coefficient \(\beta\) is the IGE. A larger value means a stronger earnings link and less relative mobility in this sample. This is an association, not a causal effect.
This Python function calculates the ordinary least-squares slope with an intercept. I average real earnings before taking logs:
import numpy as np

def slope(x, y):
    x = np.log(np.asarray(x))
    y = np.log(np.asarray(y))
    return float(np.sum((x-x.mean()) * (y-y.mean()))
                 / np.sum((x-x.mean())**2))

single = slope(sample["f2012"], sample["c2020"])
averaged = slope(sample["father_mean"], sample["child_mean"])



Dots show IGE estimates; horizontal lines show 95% confidence intervals. Both estimates use the same 336 pairs.


The single-year IGE, using father 2012 and child 2020 earnings, is 0.234, while the three-year average IGE is 0.226. Roughly, a 10% difference in fathers’ earnings is associated with a 2.3% difference in children’s earnings. The difference between estimates is small (-0.008), and its 95% bootstrap confidence interval (-0.084 to 0.050) includes zero. So, in this sample, averaging income does not clearly change the estimated relationship between fathers’ and children’s earnings.
However, this does not mean averaging is unnecessary. Income in one year may be affected by temporary changes, such as unemployment or a bonus. Averaging several years can reduce some of this variation and provide a better measure of long-run earnings. The next figure shows why the choice of year can matter.



Single-year IGE estimates using different father and child income years for the same pairs.


Choosing other years gives estimates from 0.150 to 0.240. Individual earnings changes and conditions in a particular year can affect the comparison. This shows why relying on a single year may give an incomplete picture of the earnings relationship. These differences are not all necessarily statistically significant.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 6. Check Life-Cycle Bias
A young worker may earn little while training but earn much more later. Measuring children’s earnings early in their careers could therefore give a different estimate of their earnings link with parents. Averaging several early-career years may still miss their long-run position.
I compare 140 main-sample children who also had positive 2014 earnings and were aged 22–29 at the 2015 interview. They meet the main age requirements at the later 2019/2021/2023 interviews. I keep the same father-income average in both comparisons.



IGE for the same 140 pairs at two career stages. Horizontal lines show 95% confidence intervals.


The IGE is 0.186 when children’s earnings are measured at a younger age and 0.244 when they are measured later. Mean interview age rises from 27.5 to 35.5. This suggests that measuring earnings early in a career may give a different picture of the relationship between fathers’ and children’s earnings.
However, the confidence interval for the difference (-0.111 to 0.232) includes zero, so the change is not statistically clear. Age and calendar time also change together in this comparison. The results illustrate possible life-cycle bias, but they do not prove that age caused the difference.
These unweighted results describe complete, positive-earner records, not all families. Missing follow-up, imputed income, and changing family roles also matter. We do not observe lifetime earnings.
Overall, the single-year and averaged IGE estimates are similar in this sample, but choosing different income years gives different estimates. The comparison across career stages also suggests that the age at which earnings are measured may matter, although the difference is not statistically clear. Averaging several years can reduce temporary income changes, but it cannot fully address life-cycle bias. I would not judge a family’s mobility from one convenient year.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 1. Understand the records
The Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) follows people and families. Its Parent Identification File links children to birth fathers, the Individual File tracks people, and family extracts report earnings. A permanent person ID follows someone across waves; a family ID must be paired with the interview wave because numbers recur. Python assigns Head or spouse earnings by role and adjusts income to 2022 dollars with CPI.
PSID changed this measure between the 1993 and 1994 interview waves. The 1993-wave total for 1992 included labor income from farms and unincorporated businesses; the 1994-wave measures for 1993 earnings (ER4140 and ER4144 in my extract) exclude both. My script starts with the 1995 interview and uses ER6980 and ER6984 for 1994 earnings, so it uses the post-change definition but skips the first year with that definition. The cutoff is therefore one year later than needed for comparability; adding 1993 earnings would require extending the wave map and checking the person, family, age, and role links. This matters because the later measure does not count labor income from farms or unincorporated businesses.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Step 2. Match fathers and children with SQL in Python
text:
Step 2. Match fathers and children with SQL in Python
Python prepares the tables and SQLite runs the SQL. Here, to_sql() loads tables into a temporary database; read_sql_query() sends the query to SQLite and brings the matching rows back to Python:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as con:
    chosen.to_sql("selected_earnings", con, index=False)
    sample[["child", "father"]].to_sql("eligible_links", con, index=False)
    query = Path("sql/same_age_sample.sql").read_text()
    pairs = pd.read_sql_query(query, con)
SELECT chooses needed fields. JOIN connects each father-child link to earnings summaries by permanent person ID. Before that, Python attaches income using the family ID for each interview wave. The two identifiers connect each relationship to the right people and earnings.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Step 3. Build earnings measures near age 40
text:
Step 3. Build earnings measures near age 40
I keep positive, supported earnings at interview ages 35–45 and choose observations closest to age 40. This common rule makes the generations more comparable. Interview age only approximates earnings age because income usually refers to the prior year; fathers and children can have similar ages but different income years. The single-year measure uses the closest valid year. The average uses three closest distinct years, adjusted for inflation first.
GROUP BY person gathers each person’s repeated records, and AVG() calculates mean earnings. HAVING requires three distinct years, preventing one or two observations from counting as an average:
WITH summaries AS (
  SELECT person, AVG(real_income) AS mean_income,
         AVG(age) AS mean_age,
         MAX(CASE WHEN rank = 1 THEN real_income END) AS single_income,
         MAX(CASE WHEN rank = 1 THEN age END) AS single_age
  FROM selected_earnings
  WHERE age BETWEEN 35 AND 45 AND real_income > 0
  GROUP BY person
  HAVING COUNT(*) = 3 AND COUNT(DISTINCT year) = 3
)
SELECT l.child, l.father, f.mean_income, c.mean_income,
       f.single_income, c.single_income
FROM eligible_links AS l
JOIN summaries AS f ON l.father = f.person
JOIN summaries AS c ON l.child = c.person
WHERE l.child <> l.father
  AND ABS(f.single_age - c.single_age) <= 2
  AND ABS(f.mean_age - c.mean_age) <= 2;
Both measures use the same pairs. Three valid years at ages 35–45 left 513 pairs before the age-gap rule; requiring both age gaps to be at most two years left 247 pairs (192 fathers). Mean ages remained near 40 for both generations in both measures. Requiring repeated positive earnings excludes people with missing or zero earnings, so these pairs may not represent all U.S. families. Keeping the sample fixed lets me compare the measures fairly.



Mean selected interview ages are close to 40 for fathers and children in both measures; every included pair meets the age-gap rules.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 4. Estimate and compare IGE
I estimate intergenerational earnings elasticity (IGE) by regressing log child earnings on log father earnings:
\[
\log(Y_{child}) = \alpha + \beta \log(Y_{father}) + \varepsilon
\]
The slope, beta, measures the earnings association: a one-percent difference in fathers’ earnings is associated with a beta-percent difference in children’s earnings. A larger positive value means a closer link in this sample, not a causal effect.



Single-year and three-year-average IGE estimates with 95% father-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals.


The single-year IGE is 0.067 (95% interval -0.036 to 0.217); the three-year estimate is 0.339 (0.165 to 0.504). Their paired difference is 0.272 (0.141 to 0.405), based on 2,000 father-cluster bootstrap samples that keep siblings together. The interval excludes zero. With age controls, estimates are 0.069 and 0.329, with a difference of 0.260 (0.124 to 0.392). Averaging may reduce temporary changes, but three years are still an imperfect measure of lifetime status. Since measurement age can also matter, I check one earlier comparison next.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Step 5. What does age change?
A separate check follows the same 140 pairs, comparing 2014 and 2022 child earnings against each father’s same three-year average. Mean child age rises from 27.5 to 35.5, and IGE from 0.186 to 0.244. The difference interval (-0.111 to 0.232) includes zero.



IGE estimates for the same 140 pairs when children’s earnings are measured in 2014 and 2022; age and calendar time both change.


Experience and temporary changes can make an early-career year differ from long-run earnings. This check uses 140 rather than 247 pairs, and age changes with calendar year. Its interval includes zero, so it does not establish an age effect or prove life-cycle bias. Same-age matching reduces one mismatch, but cohorts and income years still differ. The figure is suggestive, not a clean test.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
The data and the match
The PSID follows people and families. Its Parent Identification File links children to birth fathers, the Individual File tracks people, and family extracts report labor earnings. Permanent IDs track people across waves; family interview ID plus wave locates income because family numbers repeat. Python assigns Head or spouse earnings by role and converts them to 2022 dollars with CPI.
Before 1993, this income measure included farm income and the labor part of unincorporated business income. The 1993 measure and later variables exclude both. I start with 1993 earnings from the 1994 interview, the earliest comparable year in my extracts, and leave out retrospective questions with different definitions.
Python prepares the tables, and SQLite runs the SQL. to_sql() loads the prepared tables into a temporary database; read_sql_query() sends the query to SQLite and returns matched rows:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as con:
    chosen.to_sql("selected_earnings", con, index=False)
    sample[["child", "father"]].to_sql("eligible_links", con, index=False)
    query = Path("sql/same_age_sample.sql").read_text()
    pairs = pd.read_sql_query(query, con)
SELECT chooses fields. JOIN connects each father-child link to earnings summaries by permanent person ID. Before SQL, Python uses the interview wave and family ID to attach income to the right person. Without these joins, the records cannot show which father’s earnings belong with each child.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Measure earnings near age 40
The single-year measure uses the record closest to age 40; the average uses all three. Both use the same 321 pairs and 249 fathers. Keeping the sample fixed means the comparison focuses on the income measure, not different families. Interview age is an approximation because earnings usually refer to the previous calendar year.
Requiring repeated positive earnings leaves out people with zero or missing earnings. The matched families may have more stable work, so they do not represent everyone in the PSID or U.S. population.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Compare the IGE estimates
I estimate intergenerational earnings elasticity (IGE) with a log-log regression:
import numpy as np

def estimate_ige(parent_col, child_col):
    x = np.log(pairs[parent_col].to_numpy())
    y = np.log(pairs[child_col].to_numpy())
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    return np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0][1]

single_ige = estimate_ige("father_single_income", "child_single_income")
average_ige = estimate_ige("father_mean_income", "child_mean_income")
The slope measures how closely children’s earnings are associated with their fathers’. A higher IGE usually means less relative mobility. It is an association, not cause and effect.
\[
\log(Y_{child}) = \alpha + \beta\log(Y_{father}) + \varepsilon
\]



Single-year and three-year-average IGE estimates for the same 321 pairs, with 95% father-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals.


The single-year IGE is 0.170 (95% confidence interval: 0.030 to 0.354), while the three-year estimate is 0.291 (0.151 to 0.444). For example, with the three-year measure, a 1% difference in fathers’ earnings is associated with about a 0.291% difference in children’s earnings.
The higher three-year estimate suggests a stronger father-child earnings link and lower relative mobility. Both estimates use the same 321 father-child pairs, so the comparison reflects how earnings are measured rather than sample differences or a change in mobility over time.
One possible explanation is that temporary changes, such as unemployment or bonuses, make a single year’s earnings less representative of someone’s usual income. Averaging several years may reduce some of this noise. However, I cannot tell from this analysis whether temporary shocks explain the higher estimate.
The difference between the two IGEs is 0.121, with a 95% confidence interval from -0.037 to 0.268. Because the interval includes zero, I cannot confidently conclude that the two IGE estimates differ. This does not mean the two estimates are identical. Three years also cannot capture a whole career.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
What can age tell us?
A separate, older check follows 140 pairs from the earlier analysis. It compares 2014 and 2022 child earnings with each father’s three-year average. The IGE rises from 0.186 to 0.244, but the difference interval (-0.111 to 0.232) includes zero. This figure has not yet been recalculated with the 1993-inclusive sample and current selection rules.



IGE estimates for the same 140 pairs when children’s earnings are measured in 2014 and 2022; age and calendar time both change.


This is only suggestive evidence about life-cycle bias. The 140-pair sample differs from the main sample, and age changes with calendar year, so this comparison cannot isolate an age effect. A younger-age comparison may also capture different economic conditions, not just career stage.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: PSID data and the parent-child match
text:
PSID data and the parent-child match
The Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) follows families and links generations. Its Parent Identification File links children to birth fathers. The Cross-Year Individual File gives ages, roles, and family links over time. Family earnings extracts from the PSID Data Center provide labor earnings. Earnings years run from 1993 to 2022, with gaps. This analysis focuses on birth fathers and children. Mothers are not included, so the results should not be interpreted as describing all parent-child relationships.
The IDs have different jobs. A person ID follows someone over time; a family ID identifies a household in one wave and may appear again later. I first match people to that wave’s income record by family ID:
p = p.merge(fam, on="family", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
This joins each person to the household record. Household role tells Python whether the earnings belong to the Head or spouse; I do not assign the Head’s pay to everyone. SQL then uses person IDs to connect children to their fathers’ earnings.
The codebooks define these labor-income measures without farm or unincorporated-business income, which PSID records separately. I exclude retrospective measures with different definitions and adjust earnings to 2022 dollars using CPI. PSID earnings generally refer to the previous calendar year, so 1993 earnings come from the 1994 interview. See the 1993 and 1994 codebooks.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Use SQL to connect and summarize earnings
text:
Use SQL to connect and summarize earnings
Python keeps positive earnings observations at ages 35–45 and selects each person’s three distinct years closest to age 40. The closest record gets rank 1. Years need not be consecutive because PSID does not interview everyone every year. Python loads the selected records and father-child links into SQLite:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

query = Path("blog/posts/post6/sql/same_age_sample.sql").read_text()
with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as con:
    chosen.to_sql("selected_earnings", con, index=False)
    sample[["child", "father"]].to_sql("eligible_links", con, index=False)
    pairs = pd.read_sql_query(query, con)
This example runs from the website project’s root directory. The chosen and sample tables are prepared earlier in Python, with the full code available in the repository.
Here is an excerpt from the complete SQL query. It shows how the earnings summaries are made and attached to each family link:
WITH summaries AS (
  SELECT person,
         AVG(real_income) AS mean_income,
         MAX(CASE WHEN rank = 1 THEN real_income END) AS single_income
  FROM selected_earnings
  WHERE age BETWEEN 35 AND 45 AND real_income > 0
  GROUP BY person
  HAVING COUNT(*) = 3 AND COUNT(DISTINCT year) = 3
)
SELECT l.child, l.father,
       f.mean_income AS father_mean_income,
       c.mean_income AS child_mean_income,
       f.single_income AS father_single_income,
       c.single_income AS child_single_income
FROM eligible_links AS l
JOIN summaries AS f ON l.father = f.person
JOIN summaries AS c ON l.child = c.person
WHERE l.child <> l.father;
SELECT picks IDs and earnings. GROUP BY gathers each person’s records, and AVG() calculates the mean. HAVING requires three records from three distinct years. One JOIN adds the father’s earnings; the next adds the child’s. The full query also requires father and child ages to be within two years for both the single-year and average measures. The average age summarizes three interviews; it is not one exact age.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Life-cycle bias: a useful but limited check
text:
Life-cycle bias: a useful but limited check
Life-cycle bias is different from a temporary income shock. It happens because earnings at one age may not reflect someone’s long-term economic position. For example, someone studying or starting a job at 27 may earn much more later in life. Comparing fathers and children near age 40 helps make their career stages more similar, but people still follow different earnings paths. This is why matching ages cannot fully remove life-cycle bias.
For a separate group of 140 pairs, I hold fathers’ three-year average fixed and compare children’s earnings in 2014 and 2022. The IGE rises from 0.186 to 0.244 as the children’s mean interview age rises from 27.5 to 35.5. The difference is uncertain (95% confidence interval: -0.111 to 0.232).



Exploratory IGE comparison using 2014 and 2022 child earnings for a separate sample of 140 pairs. Mean interview ages are 27.5 and 35.5; age and calendar year both change.


The comparison raises the possibility that measurement age matters. But the children are older in 2022 and economic conditions have also changed since 2014. I cannot separate these explanations, so the result does not prove that age caused the IGE to rise. These 140 pairs are also separate from the main sample.
